Reduce vertical padding.

The navigation items should have
consistent horizontal spacing.

The card grid should become:

4 columns → desktop
2 columns → tablet
1 column → mobile






Specific instructions generally produce better engineering results.





  
  
  🔄 Step 6 — Iterate


A practical workflow looks like:



Reference Website
       ↓
Inspect Public Resources
       ↓
Analyze UI
       ↓
Create React Structure
       ↓
AI-Assisted Implementation
       ↓
Run Locally
       ↓
Screenshot
       ↓
Compare
       ↓
Fix
       ↓
Repeat






This isn't really “one-click cloning.”

It's an iterative reverse-engineering and reconstruction workflow.

And that's a much more useful skill to learn.





  
  
  🧠 Step 7 — What About the Backend?


This is where many tutorials become technically inaccurate.

Suppose the original website has:



Frontend
    ↓
REST API
    ↓
Backend
    ↓
PostgreSQL






You may be able to observe:



GET /api/products






and perhaps inspect the response.

But you don't automatically obtain:



backend/
├── controllers/
├── services/
├── models/
└── database/






The server executes that code remotely.


  
  
  So what should you do?


Build your own backend.

For example:



React / Next.js
       ↓
Your API
       ↓
FastAPI / Node.js
       ↓
PostgreSQL






Use your own:


database
authentication
business logic
API endpoints
environment variables


This turns a visual recreation into an actual full-stack learning project.





  
  
  🗄️ Example: Rebuilding a Product Website


Suppose the original site displays products.

You might observe:



{
  "id": 101,
  "name": "Example Product",
  "price": 49.99
}






Instead of depending on the original service, create your own API:



GET /api/products






Your backend might return:



[
  {
    "id": 1,
    "name": "Product A",
    "price": 49.99
  },
  {
    "id": 2,
    "name": "Product B",
    "price": 79.99
  }
]






Now your frontend becomes independent.

That's the correct engineering approach.





  
  
  🔐 Step 8 — Don't Copy Secrets


Never attempt to extract or reuse:



API Keys
Passwords
Private Tokens
Session Cookies
Database Credentials
Private Certificates






And don't put secrets into frontend code.

Use environment variables on your own infrastructure:



Frontend
   ↓
Your API
   ↓
Environment Variables
   ↓
Database






Security should be part of the reconstruction process from day one.





  
  
  🚀 Step 9 — Deploy Your Own Version


Once the project works locally, deploy it.

For a frontend project, platforms such as Netlify can make deployment straightforward.

Typical workflow:



Local Project
     ↓
Git Repository
     ↓
Build
     ↓
Deploy
     ↓
Live URL






You can then test the application from:



Desktop
Mobile
Tablet






and verify that your production build behaves correctly.





  
  
  ⚖️ Important: Learn From Websites, Don't Impersonate Them


There's a major difference between:


  
  
  ✅ Good use



learning frontend architecture
studying responsive layouts
recreating a generic UI
building a personal practice project
analyzing publicly delivered assets
creating your own implementation


and:


  
  
  ❌ Risky use



copying proprietary source code
extracting private backend code
reusing credentials
impersonating a company's website
copying branding or trademarks deceptively
reproducing a service for phishing or fraud


If you're publishing your recreation publicly, clearly identify it as a learning/reimplementation project.





  
  
  🧠 The Bigger Lesson


The most valuable part isn't:


“I cloned a website.”


It's:


“I learned how to analyze an existing interface and reconstruct its architecture.”


That teaches real engineering skills:



Web Architecture
       ↓
Browser DevTools
       ↓
HTTP / APIs
       ↓
Frontend Components
       ↓
Backend Design
       ↓
Database
       ↓
Testing
       ↓
Security
       ↓
Deployment






That's much more valuable than a one-click clone.





  
  
  🔥 My Recommended AI-Assisted Workflow


If I were doing this as a developer-learning project, I'd use:



1. Inspect
   ↓
2. Understand
   ↓
3. Document
   ↓
4. Rebuild
   ↓
5. Test
   ↓
6. Debug
   ↓
7. Secure
   ↓
8. Deploy






And I'd keep one rule throughout:


Use AI to accelerate implementation, not to replace understanding.






  
  
  🎯 Final Takeaway


Modern AI tools have dramatically reduced the time required to build interfaces.

But there is an important difference between:

copying a webpage

and

understanding and rebuilding a software system.

The second one teaches you much more.

Learn to inspect.

Learn to question.

Learn to reconstruct.

Learn to debug.

Learn to build your own backend.

Learn to secure it.

And finally:

Ship something that you actually understand. 🚀

Ia educacion docentes prompts chatgpt — artículo de Itelnet Consulting

Aquí tienes un artículo para dev.to, siguiendo tus indicaciones, titulado ‘5 prompts de IA que todo profesor debería usar en 2026’:





  
  
  5 prompts de IA que todo profesor debería usar en 2026


La inteligencia artificial ya no es una curiosidad tecnológica, es una herramienta con el potencial de transformar la educación. En 2026, la integración de la IA en el aula será mucho más que una simple tendencia; será una necesidad para los docentes que deseen mantener el ritmo de un mundo en constante evolución.  Pero, ¿cómo podemos aprovechar al máximo esta tecnología? No se trata de reemplazar a los profesores, sino de potenciarlos.  En este artículo, exploraremos cinco prompts de IA, diseñados específicamente para ayudar a los docentes españoles y europeos a optimizar su tiempo, mejorar sus métodos de enseñanza y fomentar un aprendizaje más personalizado.  La clave está en el ‘prompt engineering’, la habilidad de formular preguntas efectivas para obtener respuestas de calidad, y la IA, como ChatGPT, es un excelente punto de partida.


  
  
  Prompt 1: Diseño de Actividades Diferenciadas en Base a Perfiles de Aprendizaje


Uno de los mayores desafíos para los docentes es la necesidad de adaptar el contenido y las actividades a las diversas necesidades de aprendizaje de sus alumnos.  El concepto de perfiles de aprendizaje (como el modelo VARK – Visual, Auditivo, Kinestésico, y Lecto-escritura) es fundamental, pero la implementación práctica puede ser compleja.  Un prompt eficaz podría ser: “Actúa como un especialista en pedagogía diferencial. Crea una actividad de 50 minutos sobre la Revolución Francesa para un grupo de alumnos de 4º de ESO, considerando un perfil predominante visual, otro auditivo y uno kinestésico.  Incluye objetivos de aprendizaje claros, materiales sugeridos y una rúbrica de evaluación que permita diferenciar el nivel de comprensión de cada alumno.  Considera también las directrices del Ministerio de Educación en cuanto a la inclusión y la diversidad.”

Este prompt no solo genera una actividad, sino que lo hace teniendo en cuenta un marco teórico y las regulaciones educativas españolas.  El docente puede luego ajustar los resultados para que se adapten a su contexto específico y a las características de su clase.  La capacidad de generar múltiples opciones y adaptarlas es un ahorro de tiempo significativo.


  
  
  Prompt 2: Creación de Narrativas Contextualizadas para el Aprendizaje de Historia


La historia, a menudo vista como una simple acumulación de fechas y nombres, puede volverse mucho más atractiva cuando se presenta a través de narrativas.  El prompt: "Actúa como un historiador especializado en el siglo de oro español.  Escribe una narrativa de 300 palabras sobre la vida de Francisco de Quevedo, incorporando elementos de su contexto social, político y literario.  Utiliza un lenguaje accesible para alumnos de 2º de Bachillerato y propón tres preguntas de reflexión para fomentar el debate en clase."  

Este prompt no solo proporciona un texto, sino que también genera preguntas de debate, elementos esenciales para un aprendizaje activo.  La IA puede ayudar a crear una atmósfera más inmersiva y a conectar los hechos históricos con la vida de los estudiantes.  Además, el prompt puede ser ajustado para diferentes periodos históricos y niveles educativos.


  
  
  Prompt 3: Desarrollo de Rúbricas de Evaluación con Criterios de Aprendizaje Clave


La elaboración de rúbricas de evaluación es una tarea que consume mucho tiempo.  Un prompt útil sería: “Crea una rúbrica de evaluación para un proyecto de investigación sobre el impacto de la globalización en la cultura española, para alumnos de 5º de Bachillerato.  La rúbrica debe incluir criterios de evaluación en las siguientes áreas: investigación, análisis crítico, presentación oral y calidad de la redacción.  Define los niveles de desempeño (Excelente, Bueno, Satisfactorio, Necesita Mejorar) y proporciona ejemplos concretos para cada nivel en cada criterio.  Asegúrate de que la rúbrica esté alineada con los objetivos de aprendizaje del currículo de Educación Secundaria Obligatoria.”

La IA puede generar rúbricas completas y bien estructuradas, ahorrando al docente horas de trabajo y asegurando la coherencia en la evaluación.  Esto es especialmente importante en un contexto donde la legislación española exige criterios de evaluación transparentes y justos.


  
  
  Prompt 4:  Generación de Ejercicios de Práctica para el Aprendizaje de Lenguas Extranjeras


El aprendizaje de idiomas requiere mucha práctica, y la IA puede ayudar a crear ejercicios personalizados.  El prompt: “Actúa como un profesor de inglés para estudiantes de 1º de la ESO.  Crea cinco ejercicios de práctica de vocabulario relacionado con la comida y las bebidas, incluyendo ejercicios de matching, completar espacios en blanco y traducción.  Proporciona las respuestas correctas y explica la gramática relevante en cada ejercicio.”

Este prompt permite a los docentes generar material de práctica de forma rápida y sencilla, adaptado al nivel de sus alumnos.  La IA puede incluso generar ejercicios con diferentes niveles de dificultad.


  
  
  Prompt 5:  Análisis de la Legislación Educativa Española (y Europea)


La legislación educativa está en constante evolución.  Un prompt útil podría ser: "Analiza la legislación española (Ley Orgánica de Educación, LOE y su reforma, LOMLOE) sobre la inclusión de alumnos con necesidades educativas especiales, identificando los principales derechos y obligaciones de los centros educativos, los profesores y las familias.  Resume los puntos clave y proporciona enlaces a la legislación relevante."

La IA puede ayudar a los docentes a mantenerse al día con los cambios legislativos, asegurando que están cumpliendo con las normativas vigentes.  Esto es crucial en un contexto donde la legislación española y europea en materia educativa está en constante revisión.

Este curso ofrece una introducción práctica a la IA y a las técnicas de prompt engineering, con un enfoque en aplicaciones educativas.

title: Snowflake's New Coding Agent Isn't Just Another Copilot
title_hi: Snowflake's New Coding Agent Isn't Just Another Copilot
summary: The agentic era is moving from research papers to production data platforms. With the general availability of the Cortex
content:
The agentic era is moving from research papers to production data platforms. With the general availability of the Cortex Coding Agent, Snowflake is making a clear statement: agentic workflows are now a core primitive for working with data at scale. This isn't about slightly better SQL autocomplete; it's about fundamentally changing how developers build data applications by composing data-aware AI skills.


  
  
  what just shipped


In its latest release, Snowflake moved its Cortex Agents Coding Agent to general availability. This means the tool is now fully supported for production use. Alongside the agent itself, the release also includes general availability for using Cortex Extension references within agent skills. These components work together to let developers create and deploy customized, AI-powered assistants that have deep context of their organization's data environment.

Unlike a generic, standalone coding assistant, a platform-native agent operates with inherent knowledge of your data schemas, governance policies, and available services within Snowflake. The goal is not just to write code faster, but to automate entire data-centric tasks by expressing intent rather than explicit instructions.


  
  
  composing agents with skills and extensions


The real leverage here comes from the composability of the agent framework. The release notes highlight two key concepts: skills and extensions. An extension can be thought of as a tool the agent can use—a connection to an internal API, a proprietary data transformation function, or a call to another service. A skill is the agent's ability to use that tool to accomplish a specific task, often guided by a prompt that instructs the agent on how and when to use it.

This creates a powerful paradigm where you are not just prompting an LLM, but equipping it with a specific, curated set of capabilities. You move from being a prompt engineer to an agent builder. Instead of writing a complex Python script for a recurring analytics task, you might define a skill that allows the agent to perform that task on demand.

A hypothetical definition might look something like this, using SQL DDL to configure an agent:



-- Hypothetical DDL for agent creation
CREATE OR REPLACE CORTEX AGENT financial_analyst_agent
  WITH SKILLS (
    -- Skill to generate a quarterly sales report
    ( NAME = 'generate_quarterly_report',
      PROMPT = 'Given a quarter and year, use the get_sales_data_udf function to retrieve sales data and summarize it by product category. Format the output as a markdown table.',
      EXTENSION = 'get_sales_data_udf'
    ),
    -- Skill to perform fraud detection
    ( NAME = 'check_transaction_fraud',
      PROMPT = 'For the given transaction ID, use the fraud_detection_model_api to score the transaction for fraud risk. Return the risk score and a confidence level.',
      EXTENSION = 'fraud_detection_model_api'
    )
  );






This declarative approach allows you to build complex, multi-step logic that is both auditable and integrated directly with the platform's governance and security models.


  
  
  the shift to intent-based development


Making a coding agent generally available signals a durable trend. The primary interface for data interaction is moving up a layer of abstraction, from writing explicit SQL and Python to declaring intent and composing agentic capabilities. For developers, this means the focus of our work begins to shift.

Instead of writing and maintaining thousands of lines of boilerplate for data pipelines, the high-value work becomes designing robust, reliable agent skills and extensions. The challenge is no longer just about optimizing a query, but about clearly defining the boundaries and capabilities of an autonomous agent that can write and execute its own queries.

Of course, this introduces new complexities. Cost management, agent observability, and security guardrails are critical. When an agent can autonomously chain together function calls, clear monitoring and per-user quotas become essential for production stability. But the potential for leverage is immense. You are no longer just building a dashboard; you are building a virtual data analyst that your entire organization can interact with.


  
  
  so what


The GA of a platform-native coding agent is a significant milestone. It moves agents from a niche, experimental tool to a production-ready component of the modern data stack. As a builder, this is a new primitive to master. It's time to start thinking less about writing individual scripts and more about building systems of agents that can reason about and act upon your organization's data.

The AI‑generated image market has exploded over the past three years. In 2025 we have a dozen mature platforms, each targeting a slightly different niche—professional designers, hobbyists, marketers, or game developers. Prompt control, style‑locks, fine‑tuning, and API access.

Subscription vs. pay‑as‑you‑go, credits, and enterprise options.


Licensing & Commercial Rights
Whether generated assets can be sold or used in commercial projects.


Community & Ecosystem
Plugins, extensions, and active user forums.




All tools were tested on a mid‑range workstation (RTX 4090, 32 GB RAM) and via their cloud APIs where applicable. Results reflect the “standard” tier unless noted otherwise.





  
  
  1. Midjourney V6


Price – $30/mo (Basic), $60/mo (Standard), $120/mo (Pro). Unlimited generations with a “fast” GPU queue; “relaxed” mode is free but slower.  

Pros  


Unmatched artistic style; excels at fantasy, concept art, and surreal visuals.

Strong community Discord where prompt tips are shared in real time.

Consistent output across multiple aspect ratios (1:1, 16:9, 9:16).



Cons  


No native API; integration requires third‑party wrappers.

Limited control over low‑level parameters (e.g., seed, CFG scale).

Commercial licensing requires the Pro plan; otherwise images are “personal use only.”



Best For
Creative professionals who need high‑impact visuals quickly and are comfortable working in a Discord‑centric workflow.





  
  
  2. DALL·E 3 (OpenAI)


Price – $15 for 115 k credits (≈ 1 M tokens); $0.02 per additional 1 k credits. Enterprise plans start at $500/mo.  

Pros  


Extremely reliable text‑to‑image translation; handles complex prompts with fewer “hallucinations.”

Built‑in safety filters and clear commercial usage rights (images are fully owned by the user).

Seamless integration with ChatGPT, Photoshop, and Microsoft Designer via plugins.



Cons  


Slightly less stylized than Midjourney; more “photorealistic” by default.

Generation latency can spike during peak usage; premium “fast” queue costs extra credits.

Limited resolution (up to 1024 × 1024 px) without upscaling add‑ons.



Best For
Marketers, copywriters, and designers who need a dependable, API‑first solution with clear licensing.





  
  
  3. Stable Diffusion 3.0 (DreamStudio & Open‑Source Front‑Ends)


Price – DreamStudio: $12 for 1 M credits; $0.008 per extra credit. Self‑hosted: free (compute cost only).  

Pros  


Open‑source core; you can fine‑tune models on your own dataset.

Unlimited resolution via “latent upscaling” and third‑party plugins (e.g., A1111).

Strong community of extensions: ControlNet, LoRA, Prompt‑Matrix, and more.



Cons  


UI quality varies widely across front‑ends; the best experience (Automatic1111) requires technical setup.

Licensing is model‑dependent; some checkpoints are “non‑commercial.”

Out‑of‑the‑box quality can be lower than Midjourney or DALL·E without prompt engineering.



Best For
Tech‑savvy creators, indie game studios, and anyone who wants full control over model training and deployment.





  
  
  4. Adobe Firefly (Beta 2025)


Price – $29.99/mo for 1 M “generations”; enterprise tier starts at $199/mo.  

Pros  


Direct integration with Photoshop, Illustrator, and InDesign.

Firefly’s “Generative Fill” is now AI‑driven for both raster and vector assets.

Clear commercial rights: all generated content is royalty‑free for Adobe customers.



Cons  


Still in beta for some features; occasional glitches in the web UI.

Image quality leans toward “clean” illustration; less effective for gritty, hyper‑real scenes.

Requires an Adobe Creative Cloud subscription to unlock full potential.



Best For
Graphic designers already embedded in the Adobe ecosystem who need on‑the‑fly asset creation.





  
  
  5. Leonardo AI


Price – $20/mo for 200 credits (≈ 2 k images); $0.01 per extra credit. Unlimited “basic” mode for low‑resolution drafts.  

Pros  


Specialized for game art: character sheets, environment tiles, and 3D model textures.

Built‑in “Style‑Lock” that preserves a chosen aesthetic across batches.

Marketplace for buying and selling custom LoRA models.



Cons  


Limited to 1024 × 1024 px for final renders; higher resolutions need a paid “Pro” add‑on.

Community is smaller than Midjourney; fewer third‑party tutorials.

API latency can be high during peak gaming‑dev hours.



Best For
Indie game developers and concept artists who need consistent style across many assets.





  
  
  6. NightCafe Creator


Price – Free tier: 5 daily credits; $9.99/mo for 200 credits, $19.99/mo for 500 credits.  

Pros  


Very beginner‑friendly web UI with “Magic Prompt” assistance.

Supports multiple algorithms (Stable Diffusion, VQGAN‑CLIP, DALL·E 2).

Community gallery for inspiration and remixing.



Cons  


Image quality is average; not ideal for high‑end commercial work.

Credits expire after 30 days, encouraging churn.

No bulk‑upload or batch generation API.



Best For
Hobbyists and educators looking for a low‑cost entry point to AI art.





  
  
  7. Runway Gen‑2 (Video & Image)


Price – $30/mo for 100 minutes of video generation; $0.30 per extra minute. Image generation bundled at $0.02 per image.  

Pros  


First‑class video synthesis combined with still‑image generation.

Real‑time collaborative canvas for teams.

Strong AI‑assisted editing tools (background removal, motion tracking).



Cons  


Image quality still trails dedicated image‑only models.

Heavy reliance on cloud GPU; offline work is impossible.

Licensing for commercial video is still under review (as of Q2 2025).



Best For
Content creators who need both image and short‑form video generation in a single platform.





  
  
  8. Craiyon (formerly DALL·E Mini)


Price – Free, with optional $5/mo “Turbo” mode for faster queues.  

Pros  


Completely free and instantly accessible via web.

Fun for quick concept sketches and meme generation.



Cons  


Low resolution (256 × 256 px) and frequent artifacts.
